outline.description: Sets out who the parties are, why the records were sought, how the FBI processed and withheld them, and how the litigation unfolded in the district court before reaching the D.C. Circuit.
subtopics: Parties and context: Farahi’s immigration history and FBI involvement in DHS’s removal case (alleged terrorism links)
FOIA request scope and volume: approximately 10,750 pages and 80 CDs located
FBI’s initial processing, partial releases, and withholdings; missed statutory deadline leading to suit
The Hardy declarations: public and ex parte filings supporting Exemption 7(A) and categorical withholdings
District court’s November 2022 order: apparent sufficiency on 7(A) but request for updated status and segregability details due to passage of time
Renewed motion with Bender declarations (public and ex parte) confirming ongoing investigations and addressing segregability
District court’s grant of summary judgment: crediting ongoing proceedings and accepting segregability showing
Appeal to the D.C. Circuit

outline.description: Explains the FOIA statutory scheme, the elements and burdens under Exemption 7(A), the segregability mandate, evidentiary tools (affidavits and ex parte submissions), and the standard of review.
subtopics: FOIA baseline: disclosure mandate and burden on the government to justify withholdings (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(B))
Exemption 7(A): records compiled for law enforcement purposes; disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings
‘Pending or reasonably anticipated’ proceedings requirement (CREW v. DOJ)
Deference to law enforcement agencies, especially where national security is implicated (Campbell; CNSS v. DOJ)
Use of affidavits/declarations to carry the government’s burden; sufficiency and specificity standards
Segregability requirement: reasonable steps to release nonexempt portions; ‘inextricably intertwined’ doctrine (Mead; Juarez)
Categorical withholdings: categories must be sufficiently distinct (Gallant; CREW)
Ex parte, in camera submissions in national security cases and their role in FOIA adjudication
Appellate standard of review: de novo for summary judgment in FOIA cases

outline.chapter_title: Applying 7(A) Prong One: Compiled for Law Enforcement Purposes
outline.description: Details how the court found a rational nexus between the records and the FBI’s law-enforcement duties, satisfying the first requirement of Exemption 7(A).
subtopics: Rational nexus test: connection to agency law-enforcement duties and to a possible security risk or violation (Pratt; Campbell)
Hardy public declaration: investigations into national security and international terrorism, including Farahi’s associations
Hardy ex parte declaration: sealed specifics corroborating law-enforcement purpose
Contextual corroboration: Farahi’s concessions in district court about investigations into ties to designated FTOs and convicted terrorists
Court’s conclusion: deference plus record facts establish law-enforcement purpose

outline.chapter_title: Applying 7(A) Prong Two: Interference with Pending or Reasonably Anticipated Proceedings
outline.description: Explains the court’s reasoning that disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with ongoing or anticipated enforcement proceedings, and addresses the staleness argument.
subtopics: Proceedings requirement: ongoing criminal investigations qualify; government may attest to existence (CREW; Juarez)
Interference rationale: ‘tipping off’ targets about scope and direction of investigation (CNSS) as a widely accepted basis
Evidence of ongoing proceedings: Hardy’s attestation of an ongoing investigation; ex parte elaboration
Bender’s later update: confirmation that investigations remained ongoing as of March 2023
Addressing staleness: why the brief Bender declaration sufficed when read with the earlier, detailed Hardy submissions and the district court’s prior ‘seemingly’ sufficient finding
Breadth and sensitivity of the investigation (as publicly described in immigration proceedings) make ongoing status plausible
Holding on prong two: a concrete prospective enforcement proceeding exists and would be jeopardized by disclosure

outline.chapter_title: Segregability, Ex Parte Reliance, Remaining Arguments, and Disposition
outline.description: Covers the court’s approval of the FBI’s segregability showing, its acceptance of ex parte submissions, the forfeiture of the categorical-withholding challenge, and the final outcome with practical takeaways.
subtopics: Segregability standard: reasonably segregable information must be released; nonexempt snippets ‘interspersed line-by-line’ may be non-meaningful (Mead; Perioperative Services)
Bender’s supplemental ex parte showing: district court found no meaningful, reasonably segregable information
Use of ex parte declarations: plaintiff did not oppose their submission; necessity in national security FOIA disputes
Categorical withholdings challenge: requirement for sufficiently distinct categories; Farahi forfeited by not specifying overbreadth (Gallant; CREW; Khine)
Appellate disposition: de novo review affirms Exemption 7(A) withholdings and segregability determination; judgment affirmed

Practice notes: update declarations when time has passed; pair public justifications with sealed detail in sensitive cases; articulate category definitions; emphasize meaningful, not trivial, segregability
